fields.title: Story mapping: how to see what can be cut
fields.keyTakeaway: A story map turns a flat list into a set of possible releases. The first slice is not "the most important stuff," but the thinnest path that still works end-to-end.
fields.checkQuestion: Why can't you build a working release from a flat backlog sorted by priority?
fields.blocks/0/text: The key question of this node is the same, but now about the whole picture: **how individual tasks form a person's end-to-end workflow.**
fields.blocks/1/text: **What happens if you do not answer this question.** The backlog is a flat list sorted by priority. Take the top ten tasks: almost certainly, you get a set you cannot use because a step in the middle was dropped. Priority and cohesion are different things.
fields.blocks/2/subtitle: Two axes instead of one list
fields.blocks/2/items/0: **Horizontal axis**—scenario steps in the order a person goes through them. This is the backbone; it rarely changes.
fields.blocks/2/items/1: **Vertical axis**—options for completing a step, top to bottom by decreasing necessity.
fields.blocks/2/items/2: **Horizontal slice**—a release: take the top row completely, and the scenario works end-to-end.
fields.blocks/2/items/3: **An empty cell in the backbone**—not "ran out of time," but "the scenario doesn't work."
fields.blocks/3/text:
Backbone: take order → select car → assign driver → issue waybill → close trip.

First slice: manual order, selection from available list, manual assignment, waybill via PDF template, single-button close. Clunky, but the dispatcher goes end-to-end and stops keeping everything in Excel.
Second slice: auto-selection by cargo class, driver hours check, trip history.
Third slice: accounting integration, mobile access for drivers.

In a flat backlog, "auto-selection by cargo class" ranked higher than "close trip" because people shouted louder for it. With the map, you see that without closing a trip, auto-selection has nothing to connect to.
fields.blocks/4/text: If your horizontal axis is named "main screen, card, settings"—that's a navigation diagram, not a story map, and you cannot slice by it.
fields.blocks/4/title: The backbone is built on human steps, not screens
fields.blocks/5/text: A map works well for one primary scenario. When there are five roles and each has its own path, a single map turns into a wall nobody reads—it's better to draw several. And a map doesn't prioritize: it shows what **can** be sliced without losing cohesion, while the decision on what to cut remains yours.
